header: IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD
PRESENT: Mr. Habib Ullah, Advocate alongwith Petitioner
Syed Ameer Ali Shah, Ch. Zaheer Ahmed and Ch.
Mr. Amjad Ali, Deputy District Attorney, ICT.
Usman Rasool Ghumman , Assistant Attorney General
body: SHAHRUKH ARJUMAND, J. Through the instant constitutional petition, the petitioner has made the following prayer: - “a. Declare all the impugned actions, orders and proceedings of the respondents either written or verbal including unlawful sealing of the petitioner's property residential House No.06, Street No.154, Sector G- 13/4, Islamabad as illegal, arbitrary, without lawful authority, of no legal effect and violation of the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution;
b. Direct the respondents to immediately de-seal the aforesaid residential premises and restored to the petitioner and his family members to peaceful possession and use thereof;

c. Direct the respondents to immediately return the articles, goods, cash, jewelry, electronic gadgets, laptop, educational certificates of children and documents of vehicles to the petitioner that they have taken from the sealed residential premises;

d. Direct the respondents to ensure that the petitioner shall not be dispossessed, evicted or otherwise deprived of the use and enjoyment of the residential property in violation of the interim order dated 12.02.2026 passed by the Honourable Peshawar High Court Peshawar; Page 2 of 53 e. Direct the respondents to provide the petitioner and his family immediate access to their personal belongings, educational documents, academic records, books, laptops and other essential articles lying inside the sealed premises;
f. Direct the respondents to refrain/restrain from harassing, or taking any adverse action against the petitioner and his family members qua the above mentioned residential property.
g. Direct the respondent No.1 to initiate departmental disciplinary and other proceedings against the respondent No.2 and its employees according to law.”

2. The facts giving rise to the instant constitutional petition, as set out by the petitioner, are that he claims to be the lawful owner of ancestral land measuring 05 kanals and 02 marlas, comprised in Khata/Khatooni No. 513/590, Khasra Nos. 342/2/6 and 343/1/5, situated in the revenue estate of Village Mauza Bagra, Tehsil and District Haripur. According to the petitioner, with a view to shifting his residence to Islamabad, he entered into an exchange arrangement in January 2023 in respect of the said ancestral property for House No. 06, Street No. 154, Sector G-13/4, Islamabad, on the representation that the house was free from any dispute or encumbrance. At the relevant time, the house stood in the name of Danish Wahab son of Wilayat Khan, stated to be its original owner, who had entered into a sale agreement with Hakeem Khan; thereafter, pursuant to the exchange transaction, the house was transferred in favour of the petitioner, who was also delivered peaceful and vacant physical possession thereof. The petitioner relies upon the sale deed, transfer deed, power of attorney, Certificate of Transfer and letter of transfer of allotment, stated to have been executed on 13.11.2023, in support of his title and possession. He asserts that he thereafter continued to reside in the premises with his family as its lawful owner and remained in peaceful possession thereof until he received, on 28.09.2025, a call-up notice dated 24.09.2025 from the National Accountability Bureau (NAB), requiring him to appear before the Combined Investigation Team-I, Investigation Wing-I, NAB (KP), Peshawar, on 01.10.2025 along with the relevant record, whereupon he came to know of the NAB proceedings concerning one Qaisar Khan. The petitioner states that he appeared before NAB, recorded his statement and explained that Page 3 of 53 Qaisar Khan had transferred the house to him against exchange of the aforesaid ancestral land; according to him, the Investigating Officer acknowledged his ownership of the property and assured him that his rights therein would be protected. Subsequently, the petitioner came to know that his property had been frozen pursuant to proceedings before the NAB authorities and the Accountability Court and, being aggrieved, instituted W.P. No. 5197/2025 before this Court seeking, inter alia, setting aside of the orders dated 05.11.2025 and 12.11.2025, defreezing of the property and suspension of the proceedings relating thereto. On 11.12.2025, this Court, while considering the said petition and the accompanying C.M. No. 1/2025, directed, inter alia, that the petitioner should not be dispossessed from the property, namely House No. 06, Street No. 154, Sector G-13, Islamabad, until the next date of hearing. The petition, however, came to be dismissed on 26.01.2026 for want of jurisdiction, the Court observing that the impugned orders dated 05.11.2025 and 12.11.2025 had been passed by the concerned NAB authorities and Accountability Court at Peshawar. The petitioner thereafter approached the Peshawar High Court through W.P. No. 10462-P/2025, accompanied by I.R. C.M. No. 536/2025, which, vide order dated 02.07.2026, was converted into an objection petition under Section 13 of the NAB Ordinance against the order dated 12.11.2025 passed by Accountability Court-III, Peshawar, and the record was directed to be transmitted to the said Court. During the pendency of the objection petition, the petitioner states that he proceeded to his native village during the summer vacation of his children and, in his absence, on 29.07.2026, the Magistrate, Humak, Islamabad, allegedly broke open the locks of the main gate of the aforesaid house, replaced them with other locks and sealed the premises without prior notice to the petitioner or, according to him, any court or sealing order having been furnished to him. The petitioner further states that, at the time of sealing, various household articles and valuables were lying inside the premises, including furniture, electronic equipment, approximately 10 tolas of gold ornaments, cash amounting to Rs.550,000/-, two vehicles, namely Suzuki Alto and Khyber, original documents, the educational certificates of his children, a laptop and other valuable articles. According to the petitioner, on 17.08.2026, his neighbour informed him that the entrance locks of the property had been opened and a window was also found open; he consequently alleges that, notwithstanding the sealing of the premises, employees associated with the office of the Magistrate Page 4 of 53 had repeatedly visited the house, opened its locks and remained there without lawful authority, resulting, according to him, in the removal or misappropriation of various valuables kept inside the premises. The petitioner states that he brought the matter to the notice of the SHO, Police Station Sumbal, Islamabad, who allegedly recorded a video of the condition of the premises and contacted the concerned authorities, whereafter an employee, namely Bilal, was sent to the site but, according to the petitioner, failed to ensure proper locking and security of the premises. The petitioner thereafter submitted an application to the concerned respondent, alleging negligence, misconduct, misuse and abuse of official authority in relation to the safeguarding of the property and the articles lying therein, but asserts that no effective action was taken thereon. Meanwhile, on 04.08.2026, the petitioner instituted W.P. No. 11857-P/2026 before the Peshawar High Court against NAB and other respondents, wherein, according to him, despite the appearance of NAB, no sealing order was produced before the Court nor was the Court apprised of any judicial order authorizing the sealing of the property at Islamabad. The said petition was disposed of on 13.08.2026, with the Peshawar High Court observing that the sealing had been carried out by the Magistrate on the directions of NAB, but that there was no material on record establishing that any order had in fact been passed by a Court within that jurisdiction authorizing the sealing of the premises, and the petitioner was accordingly left to approach the appropriate forum at Islamabad. The petitioner, maintaining that he has no connection with or liability in respect of the NAB proceedings against Qaisar Khan and that the property in question was acquired by him through a bona fide exchange of his ancestral land, has accordingly called in question the freezing and subsequent sealing of the property, as well as the acts and omissions attributed by him to the respondents in relation thereto, and seeks appropriate constitutional relief, including de-sealing of the premises and protection of his asserted proprietary and possessory rights therein.

3. Learned counsel for the petitioner, while assailing the impugned actions of the respondents, contended that the freezing and sealing of the petitioner's property, and the consequential deprivation of his possession and use thereof, were wholly without lawful authority, jurisdiction or legal justification and amounted to an arbitrary, mala fide, disproportionate and colourable exercise of power, in Page 5 of 53 violation of Articles 4, 9, 10-A, 14 and 25 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973. It was argued that the petitioner, being a bona fide purchaser and lawful owner, could not be subjected to adverse consequences arising from any alleged wrongdoing attributable to another person, particularly in the absence of any allegation or material establishing his knowledge, participation, connivance or nexus with the alleged unlawful acquisition or source of the property. Learned counsel further submitted that the respondents had failed to identify any lawful provision authorizing the impugned deprivation or to demonstrate compliance with the requirements of due process, notice and lawful procedure, and that the impugned action, therefore, constituted an impermissible interference with the petitioner's proprietary, possessory, residential, privacy and dignity rights. It was contended that the respondents were bound to exercise their statutory powers strictly within the confines of law and could not, under the guise of proceedings against another person, extend the consequences thereof to an innocent third party without first establishing the requisite legal basis and nexus. Learned counsel also alleged that the officials concerned had failed in their legal duty to safeguard the property and its contents and that valuable articles belonging to the petitioner had been removed or misappropriated, warranting appropriate legal action. It was lastly argued that the impugned actions were founded upon conjectures and surmises rather than lawful material, that the respondents had failed to properly appreciate the petitioner's asserted title and independent legal status, and that the petitioner could not, in law, be made to suffer for any alleged wrongdoing of another; consequently, the impugned actions and orders, being contrary to law, facts and constitutional guarantees, were liable to be declared without lawful authority and set aside.

4. Learned counsel for the respondents, while opposing the petition, raised a preliminary objection to its maintainability, contending that the petitioner had already invoked the statutory remedy available under Section 13 of the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999 in respect of the very property and dispute in question and that the said proceedings, having been converted from W.P. No. 10462-P/2025 and transmitted to the learned Accountability Court-III, Peshawar, were still pending; consequently, the petitioner could not simultaneously invoke the extraordinary constitutional jurisdiction of this Court for substantially the same grievance or seek parallel relief from different forums. It was argued that the Page 6 of 53 principal controversy concerning the freezing/attachment of the property emanated from the proceedings initiated by NAB (KP) and the orders passed by the competent authorities at Peshawar, whereas the sealing of the property at Islamabad was merely consequential thereto, rendering the Accountability Court seized of the matter the appropriate forum to determine all questions relating to the status and treatment of the property. Learned counsel further contended that the petitioner was estopped by his own conduct from maintaining the present proceedings, having approbated and reprobated before different forums, and that the petition was liable to be dismissed as an abuse of the process of law, particularly as the petitioner had allegedly failed to make a full and candid disclosure of the pending statutory proceedings and had approached this Court without clean hands. It was also urged that the petition suffered from misjoinder and non-joinder of necessary parties, particularly NAB (KP), whose proceedings and interests would directly be affected by any order concerning the de-sealing or status of the property. On the merits, learned counsel submitted that the property had been frozen in exercise of powers under Section 12 of the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999, on account of its alleged connection with the investigation/proceedings against Qaisar Khan and that the petitioner's assertion of bona fide ownership or purchase was itself a disputed question pending adjudication before the competent Accountability Court. Learned counsel emphatically denied the allegations of theft, misappropriation or removal of gold, cash, vehicles, electronic equipment or other articles from the premises, characterizing such allegations as unsubstantiated and disputed questions of fact requiring evidence, examination of witnesses, documentary material and, where necessary, forensic inquiry, matters which, according to learned counsel, could not appropriately be adjudicated in the summary jurisdiction of this Court under Article 199 of the Constitution. It was further submitted that, prior to the freezing of the property, an inventory of the articles therein had been prepared in the presence of a representative of NAB (KP) and a police official of Police Station Sumbal, thereby contradicting the allegation that the property or its contents had been left unsecured or unaccounted for. It was lastly contended that the petition is false, frivolous and motivated by ulterior considerations, that the petitioner had failed to establish any violation of his fundamental rights or any exercise of authority in excess of jurisdiction, and that, in view of the availability and Page 7 of 53 pendency of the statutory remedy, the disputed nature of the allegations and the alleged non-joinder and suppression of material facts, the constitutional petition was liable to be dismissed.
5. Arguments I have heard, while record also perused.

6. The first question requiring determination is whether, notwithstanding the fact that the property in dispute is situated in Islamabad, territorial jurisdiction in relation to the impugned proceedings is to be determined solely with reference to the situs of the property, or whether the matter is governed by the special jurisdictional regime prescribed under the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999. The issue assumes significance because proceedings concerning the property were initiated by NAB and the reference/proceedings are pending before the learned Accountability Court at Peshawar. It therefore becomes necessary to examine the relevant provisions of the NAO in light of authoritative pronouncements of the Superior Courts, particularly those governing the institution and trial of references, and to determine whether the Chairman NAB possesses statutory discretion to institute a reference before the competent Accountability Court in a particular territorial jurisdiction or otherwise.

Scope and effect of Section 16(e) of the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999 7. The starting point of the analysis is Section 16 of the Ordinance, which is a special provision dealing specifically with the case management and trial of offences falling within the ambit of the accountability regime. Before diving in the detailed analysis of the NAB statutory scheme, for the sake of reference, the Section 16 of the Ordinance is reproduced as under: - “16. Case management and trial of offences. (a) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, an accused shall be prosecuted for an offence under this Ordinance in the Court established under this Ordinance and the case shall be disposed of within one year.
(b) The Court shall sit at such place or places as the Federal Government may, by order, specify in this behalf.

Page 8 of 53 (c) Where more Courts than one have been established at a place, the Chief Justice of the High Court of the Province concerned shall designate a Judge of any such Court to be an administrative Judge and a case triable under this Ordinance shall be filed before the Court of the Administrative Judge who may either try the case himself or, assign it for trial by any other court established at that place at any time prior to the framing of the charge.

(d) In respect of a case assigned to a Court under sub-section (c), all orders made or proceedings taken before the assignment shall be deemed to have been made or taken by the Court to which the case has been assigned.

(e) Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, if in respect of any case relating to an offence triable under this Ordinance, the Chairman NAB, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case may file a reference before any Court established anywhere in Pakistan, and such Court shall have the jurisdiction to try the same.”

8. The provision is not couched in uncertain, qualified or restrictive terms. Rather, it provides in express and unequivocal language that, notwithstanding anything contained in Section 16, where a case relates to an offence triable under the Ordinance, the Chairman NAB, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, may file a reference before any Court established anywhere in Pakistan, and such Court shall have the jurisdiction to try the same. The provision, therefore, contains two distinct but interrelated components: first, it confers upon the Chairman NAB a statutory discretion concerning the forum before which a reference may be instituted; and secondly, it expressly attaches jurisdiction to the Court before which such reference is filed in accordance with the statutory discretion. Both components are required to be given full meaning and effect, for the Court is not at liberty to disregard any part of the legislative command or to substitute a limitation which the legislature itself has not enacted.

9. The expression “notwithstanding anything contained in this section” constitutes the first important indicator of legislative intent. It is a non obstante clause employed to give the succeeding provision overriding effect over the other provisions contained in Section 16. Subsections (a) to (d) principally establish the Page 9 of 53 ordinary institutional and procedural arrangement governing Accountability Courts: prosecution before a Court established under the Ordinance, the place at which such Court shall sit, the designation of an Administrative Judge where more than one Court exists at a particular place, and the consequences of assignment of a case from one Court to another. Clause (e), however, deliberately begins by declaring that its operation shall prevail notwithstanding anything contained in the preceding provisions of the section. The legislative choice is therefore significant: while the earlier clauses establish the ordinary framework, clause (e) creates a specific and overriding rule for the selection of the forum in an appropriate accountability case. It would defeat the very purpose of the non obstante expression if clause (e) were interpreted as merely repeating the ordinary territorial arrangement contained in the preceding clauses (overriding of Special law upon general law shall be discussed at a later stage in this judgment).

10. The second expression of decisive significance is “having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case”. This entrusted the Chairman NAB with discretion to determine the appropriate forum after taking into consideration the circumstances attending the particular case. The discretion is neither unstructured nor arbitrary; it is statutorily anchored to the facts and circumstances of the case. The phrase necessarily imports an obligation to apply mind to the peculiar features of the matter before exercising the statutory power. It may encompass, depending upon the nature of the case, the place where material transactions occurred, the location of relevant records and evidence, the persons involved, the public authority or public funds affected, the convenience and effectiveness of investigation and prosecution, the number and location of accused persons and witnesses, the relationship between different transactions forming part of one investigation, and other circumstances which may legitimately bear upon the efficacious prosecution of an accountability offence. What is important for present purposes is that the legislature did not make the situs of the alleged offence the sole statutory criterion for determining the forum. Had that been the legislative intention, it could readily have employed language expressly confining the filing of a reference to the Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the offence was committed. Instead, the legislature adopted the broader formulation that the Chairman NAB, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, may file Page 10 of 53 the reference before “any Court established anywhere in Pakistan.” The breadth of the phrase “any Court established anywhere in Pakistan” cannot be overlooked or reduced to surplusage. The ordinary meaning of “any” is expansive, and the words “any Court established anywhere in Pakistan” manifest a legislative choice to avoid restricting the Chairman NAB to the territorial limits of the place where the alleged offence, transaction, accused or property may be situated. The expression is nationwide in its geographical reach. It does not say “any Court within the territorial jurisdiction where the offence was committed”; nor does it say “any Court within the Province concerned”; nor does it require that the Court selected by the Chairman NAB should have an otherwise existing territorial nexus with the alleged offence. The only statutory qualification is that the Court must be a Court established under the Ordinance and that the Chairman must exercise his discretion having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case. Once these statutory conditions are fulfilled, the provision itself declares that the Court before which the reference is filed “shall have the jurisdiction to try the same.” In the present case, the relevance of the expression “facts and circumstances of the case” is further reinforced by the very nature and genesis of the underlying accountability proceedings. The reference arises out of the alleged Kohistan scandal, the foundational allegations and alleged financial irregularities being rooted in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Thus, even when the matter is examined from the standpoint of the geographical nexus of the alleged occurrence and the circumstances giving rise to the accountability proceedings, there exists a substantial and direct connection with Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The place where the alleged underlying events occurred, the origin of the allegations, the investigative material and the proceedings arising therefrom constitute circumstances which were legitimately capable of being taken into account by the Chairman NAB while determining the appropriate forum under Section 16(e). The fact that a particular asset subsequently came to be situated in Islamabad does not displace or diminish that nexus. On the contrary, the circumstances attending the underlying case, viewed as a whole, furnish a rational and legally cognizable basis for the institution and continuation of the reference before the competent Accountability Court at Peshawar.

11. The concluding words of clause (e) are equally significant. The legislature has not merely authorized the Chairman NAB to present or lodge a reference Page 11 of 53 before a Court situated elsewhere; it has gone further and expressly provided that “such Court shall have the jurisdiction to try the same.” The word “shall” ordinarily carries a mandatory character, and, in the context in which it has been employed, it leaves little room for treating the jurisdiction of the selected Court as merely provisional, contingent or subject to the general territorial rules applicable to ordinary criminal proceedings. The statutory consequence of a reference validly filed under clause (e) is therefore expressly stated by the legislature itself: the Court before which the reference is filed acquires jurisdiction to try that reference. This interpretation is further reinforced by the relationship between Section 16(e) and Section 18 of the Ordinance. Section 18 regulates the taking of cognizance by an Accountability Court and establishes the reference as the statutory mechanism through which the accountability jurisdiction of the Court is invoked. The two provisions must therefore be read harmoniously. Section 16(e) determines the permissible forum in which the reference may be instituted, while Section 18 regulates the assumption of cognizance upon such reference. The statutory scheme consequently does not contemplate that, after the Chairman NAB has exercised the discretion expressly conferred by Section 16(e) and the reference has been filed before a Court falling within the statutory description, the jurisdiction of that Court may nevertheless be defeated merely by invoking a general principle of territoriality which the special provision itself has displaced. This becomes particularly important in cases involving recovery, tracing, freezing or attachment of assets. The place where an asset is eventually located is not necessarily the place where the underlying corruption or corrupt practice occurred. An accountability investigation may originate from an offence committed in one part of the country, while the proceeds, investments, properties, bank accounts, securities or other assets connected with that offence may subsequently be found in several different jurisdictions. If the location of every such asset were treated as independently determinative of the territorial jurisdiction of the Accountability Court, a single reference could become subject to multiple and potentially conflicting jurisdictions. Section 16(e), by expressly permitting the Chairman NAB to select Accountability Court anywhere in Pakistan and by declaring that the selected Court shall possess jurisdiction to try the reference, provides a statutory answer to precisely such a problem.

Page 12 of 53 12. The legislative history of Section 16 further strengthens this interpretation. The provision quoted before me was introduced through the National Accountability (Amendment) Act, 2022, which expressly substituted Section 16 and retained, in subsection (e), the formulation empowering the Chairman NAB, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, to file a reference before any Court established anywhere in Pakistan, with jurisdiction thereby vesting in such Court. The Gazette of Pakistan dated 22 June 2022 records the substitution of Section 16 and reproduces the very language presently under consideration. The significance of this legislative history is that the nationwide forum-selection power was not merely an accidental survival from an obsolete statutory text; rather, the legislature, while substituting the entire provision, consciously retained the substance of the power in clause (e).

13. The judicial interpretation and application of this statutory provision by the superior Courts provide further guidance on the scope and effect of the jurisdictional framework embodied in Section 16 of the Ordinance. The superior Courts have consistently recognized that, once a NAB reference is filed before an Accountability Court and cognizance is taken, the proceedings fall within the exclusive domain of that Court. The constitutional jurisdiction of a High Court must, therefore, be examined with reference to the territorial jurisdiction of the Court seized of the reference, rather than merely the location of an asset connected with the proceedings. In PLD 2015 Sindh 1[Re. Aqeel Kareem Dhedhi Vs. Chairman NAB and 3 Others], it was held: - “Muhammad Ashraf (supra), decided by honourable Supreme Court by order dated 13-11-2013, wherein the facts of the case are that the petitioner was facing trial under National Accountability Ordinance 1999 before the Accountability Court No.1 Lahore. He filed Constitution Petition before the Islamabad High Court, impleading the National Accountability Bureau, the Special Judge Accountability Court No.1, Lahore, The Special Prosecutor General, NAB and others, praying, inter alia,. that the Court be directed to dismiss the prosecution case against the petitioner. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, while holding that the matter falls within the territorial jurisdiction of the Lahore High Court where the petitioner is facing trial. Thus the petitioner preferred leave to appeal against such Page 13 of 53 judgment of the Islamabad High Court and Hon'ble apex Court while deciding such petition observed as under:-- "The Contention of the learned counsel has no merits. We will refrain from dilating upon the decision of this Court in Criminal Appeals Nos.140 of 2005 etc. as the High Court had not touched upon the same but dismissed the petitioner's constitution petition for want of territorial jurisdiction. We tend to agree with the High Court. Once the Chairman of the National Accountability Bureau had filed the Reference and cognizance was taken thereof by the Accountability Court the case thereafter falls within the exclusive domain of the Court. The prayer for direction to the Chairman National Accountability Bureau and the Prosecutors could thus not be granted as the case is now under trial before the Accountability Court. The said court falls within the territorial jurisdiction of the Lahore High Court. The High Court under Article 199 of the Constitution can take cognizance of all matters that falls within its territorial iurisdiction and not bevond it The Islamabad High Court rightly declined to exercise jurisdiction in the matter. The petition, is therefore, dismissed and leave declined.”

14. While concluding the above case, the Court held that the jurisdiction of a High Court of a Province, in relation to proceedings under the Ordinance, is confined to the Accountability Courts situated within its territorial jurisdiction and does not extend to Courts established beyond it. This conclusion was reinforced by Section 32(a), which expressly provides that an appeal against the final judgment of an Accountability Court lies before the High Court of the Province where that Court is situated; any contrary interpretation would defeat the statutory scheme governing the administrative and appellate jurisdiction of the High Courts under the Ordinance. The Court held that: - “It is patent that the provisions without any ambiguity confines the jurisdiction of High Court of a Province to the 'Courts' established within its jurisdiction and not beyond that. This legal position stands further clear from subsection (a) of section 32 of the Ordinance which specifies that:

Page 14 of 53 (a) Any person convicted or the Prosecutor General Accountability, if so directed by (the Chairman) NAB) aggrieved by the final judgment and order of the Court under this Ordinance may within ten days of the final judgment and order of the Court prefer an Appeal to the High Court of the Province where the court is situated)

19. In view of above legal position, if the plea of the petitioner is sustained that this Court can competently quash the proceeding of reference, pending before the Court at Islamabad it shall mean to frustrate the very meaning, purpose and object of the above provision (s) of the Ordinance which limits the administrative or appellate jurisdiction of a High Court of a Province for Courts, established within its jurisdiction only. This view stood stamped by honourable Supreme Court in above referred unreported Judgment.
20. Accordingly, we find that petition, in hand, is not maintainable on the point of jurisdiction and same is dismissed in limine.”

15. The existence of Section 16-A does not detract from this conclusion. On the contrary, the transfer mechanism contained therein complements Section 16(e). Section 16(e) addresses the initial selection of the forum by the Chairman NAB, whereas Section 16-A provides a statutory mechanism for transferring cases in circumstances contemplated by the Ordinance. The existence of a transfer mechanism presupposes that a case may validly commence before an Accountability Court having jurisdiction under the Ordinance and that its movement thereafter must take place through the statutory mechanism. It would be incongruous to read Section 16-A as impliedly nullifying the express jurisdiction conferred by Section 16(e), when both provisions form part of the same special statutory scheme. Nor can the ordinary rules governing territorial jurisdiction under general criminal law be employed to defeat the express command of Section 16(e). The principle that a criminal offence is ordinarily tried where it is committed is a rule of general application. Section 16(e), however, is a special statutory provision enacted specifically for offences falling within the accountability regime and contains an express departure from that general rule. The settled interpretative principle that a special provision prevails over a general provision therefore becomes relevant. The maxim generalia specialibus non derogant is not being Page 15 of 53 invoked to create jurisdiction where none exists; rather, it is being applied to give effect to a jurisdiction which the legislature has expressly created through the special enactment.

16. The constitutional dimension also merits consideration. The conferment of forum-selection authority upon the Chairman NAB does not mean that such discretion is beyond legal scrutiny. The power must be exercised bona fide, for the purposes contemplated by the Ordinance, and having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case. An exercise of statutory discretion motivated by extraneous considerations, mala fides, discrimination or an abuse of authority may undoubtedly invite judicial review on an appropriate factual and legal foundation. What, however, cannot be done is to convert the existence of discretion into an absence of jurisdiction. The statute itself determines the legal consequence of a valid exercise of that discretion: the Court selected in accordance with Section 16(e) shall have jurisdiction to try the case. The provision must also be understood in light of the nature and purpose of the National Accountability Ordinance. Accountability proceedings frequently involve complex financial transactions extending across provincial and territorial boundaries, multiple accused persons, public funds, corporate structures, immovable properties, banking transactions and documentary evidence dispersed across different parts of the country. A rigid requirement that every constituent act or every connected asset must be litigated exclusively at its individual physical location could fragment a single investigation into multiple proceedings before different Courts. Such fragmentation would not only burden the administration of justice but could also produce inconsistent findings concerning the same factual matrix. The legislative conferral of a nationwide forum-selection power upon the Chairman NAB, subject to consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, can therefore be understood as an instrument designed to preserve coherence, efficiency and effectiveness in the prosecution of complex accountability cases.

17. The foregoing interpretation also finds persuasive support in comparative jurisprudence. In Rana Ayyub v. Directorate of Enforcement through its Assistant Director, 2023 SCC OnLine SC 109, the Supreme Court of India was confronted with a question concerning the territorial jurisdiction of a Special Court constituted under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), in circumstances Page 16 of 53 where the relevant events and assets were spread across different territorial jurisdictions. The petitioner had initiated three crowdfunding campaigns during the COVID-19 pandemic through an online platform, Ketto, whereupon the Mumbai Zonal Office of the Enforcement Directorate initiated an investigation against her on 03.08.2021. Meanwhile, a private complaint was lodged at Ghaziabad on 07.09.2021 and registered as an FIR, on the basis of which the Delhi office of the Enforcement Directorate registered proceedings against the petitioner under the PMLA before the Special Judge at Ghaziabad. During the pendency of the investigation being conducted by the Mumbai Zonal Office, a bank account of the petitioner maintained at Navi Mumbai was attached under the provisions of the PMLA, and subsequently, on 29.11.2022, the Special Court issued summons requiring her appearance on 13.12.2022. The petitioner challenged the jurisdiction of the Special Court, contending that, in view of Section 44 of the PMLA, the case ought to have been dealt with by the court having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the offence was committed and that, since the attached bank account was situated at Navi Mumbai and no part of the alleged offence had been committed within the jurisdiction of the Special Court, the proceedings were without territorial competence. The Enforcement Directorate, on the other hand, contended that the court which had taken cognizance of the scheduled offence was competent to take cognizance of the proceedings under the PMLA. Upon examination of Sections 43 and 44 of the PMLA, the Supreme Court identified the distinction between cases where the scheduled offence and the offence of money laundering were committed within the jurisdiction of the same court and cases where they were committed within the jurisdiction of different courts, and observed that the statutory scheme of Section 44 required the scheduled offence to follow the offence of money laundering for purposes of territorial jurisdiction, rather than the converse. The Court further held that although the general provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure ordinarily govern territorial jurisdiction, those provisions must yield where the special statute makes a specific provision regulating the jurisdiction of the court. While considering the territorial competence of the Special Court, the Supreme Court noted that criminal jurisdiction may, depending upon the nature of the offence, be attracted by various connecting factors, including the place where the offence is committed, the place where its consequences are felt, the location of the accused or victim, and the Page 17 of 53 location of property connected with the offence. However, in the context of the PMLA, the Court emphasized that the mere existence or attachment of a bank account at Navi Mumbai could not, by itself, conclusively determine the place of commission of the offence, particularly where the statutory ingredients of money laundering included acts such as concealing, possessing, acquiring, using, projecting or claiming proceeds of crime as untainted, which might occur at different places. The Court was further persuaded by the fact that the transactions had been conducted through an online platform and that the questions concerning possession, acquisition and use of the alleged proceeds involved factual matters requiring determination by the Special Court seized of the proceedings and could not appropriately be resolved summarily in collateral proceedings. The petition was consequently dismissed, leaving the petitioner at liberty to raise her jurisdictional objections before the Special Judge. The ratio is of persuasive relevance to the controversy before this Court insofar as it demonstrates that, in the context of complex financial offences governed by a special statutory regime, the physical location of a particular asset or account cannot, in isolation, be treated as the sole or determinative basis for conferring territorial jurisdiction, where the statutory scheme connects the adjudication of the asset with the broader offence and proceedings of which it forms part.

18. Applying the foregoing principles to the facts at hand, the freezing of the property, the alleged sealing thereof, and every consequential question touching its status are inextricably bound up with the reference/proceedings pending before the Accountability Court at Peshawar, itself seized of the matter pursuant to a reference instituted, on the record before us, in the exercise of the Chairman NAB's discretion under Section 16(e). It is a settled principle of statutory construction that a special law, enacted to regulate a particular subject in a comprehensive or specialized manner, prevails over a general law to the extent of inconsistency, expressed in the maxim lex specialis derogat legi generali. The principle does not mean that general law becomes wholly irrelevant; rather, it means that where the legislature has consciously enacted a special rule addressing the precise subject-matter in question, the Court is required to give effect to that special rule instead of importing a general rule which would qualify, restrict or defeat the legislative scheme. The present constitutional jurisdiction is not intended to authorize orders against persons or authorities who are directly affected by the adjudication without affording them an opportunity of hearing. Indeed, Article 199 itself contemplates relief against a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Federation, a Province or a local authority, and the identity of the authority responsible for the impugned act is therefore of fundamental significance to the exercise of jurisdiction.

53. The principle is reinforced by the nature of the relief sought in the instant case. The petitioner is not merely complaining of an independent ministerial act of the local administration concerning an otherwise unrelated property. His own case is that the property has been subjected to sealing in connection with the accountability proceedings, and the order relied upon by him expressly records that the sealing was carried out on the directions of NAB. The Court, therefore, cannot effectively determine the petitioner's grievance without examining the role, authority and conduct of NAB. Here the principle of audi alteram partem reinforces. The maxim audi alteram partem, literally meaning “hear the other side,” constitutes one of the foundational principles of natural justice. It embodies the elementary requirement that no judicial, quasi-judicial or administrative determination carrying adverse civil consequences should ordinarily be made against a person without giving such person notice of the proceedings and a Page 51 of 53 meaningful opportunity to present his case. The principle is not a mere technicality of procedure; rather, it is directed towards ensuring fairness, impartiality and legitimacy in the decision-making process. A Court, while exercising jurisdiction, is required to hear all those persons whose rights or interests are likely to be directly affected by the order proposed to be passed, particularly where the relief sought cannot effectively be granted without determining matters concerning such person. The rule assumes greater significance where the person sought to be affected is not merely a remote or interested party, but is the very authority or person responsible for the act or order under challenge. In such circumstances, the Court cannot ordinarily adjudicate upon the legality, propriety or justification of that action behind the back of the person who took it or is legally responsible for defending it. The requirement of hearing is founded upon both fairness to the affected party and the institutional necessity of enabling the Court to have before it all relevant facts, explanations and legal submissions bearing upon the controversy. In PLD 2025 SC 11, the Hon’ble Supreme Court observed that: - “14. Furthermore, Article 10A of the Constitution requires that everyone is entitled to a fair trial and due process, which includes the basic right to be heard 20 The principle of 'audi alteram partem' is one of the foundational principles of natural justice. It necessitates the requirement of being heard so that the judicial order reflects the contention of every party before the court. To fulfill the requirements of being heard, it is settled that the relevant party must be issued first a notice and then be allowed a hearing 21 These two (notice and hearing) are basic pre-requisites, which satisfy the test of being heard as well as fair trial and due process within the ambit of Article 10A of the Constitution. In this matter, it appears that the Impugned Judgment and Impugned Order have not given an opportunity of hearing to the concerned parties which include the federal government and the affectees of the Revised Policy. This amounts to a violation of their basic right to be heard and suggests that the decision was made without following due process.”

54. The doctrine is closely connected with the concept of a necessary party. A necessary party is one in whose absence no effective and binding adjudication can properly be made, particularly where the proposed order would directly operate Page 52 of 53 upon such party's rights, obligations, authority or conduct. The requirement of joinder, therefore, is not merely a matter of procedural convenience. It serves the substantive purpose of ensuring that a person against whom an order may operate is brought before the Court and afforded an opportunity to defend the legality of the action attributed to him. An order passed in the absence of such a party may not only occasion prejudice to that party but may also render the adjudication incomplete and vulnerable to challenge. In 2021 SCMR 369, the Hon’ble Supreme Court emphasized that a proceeding founded upon equity cannot be adjudicated without affording the affected person an opportunity of hearing. “----'Audi alteram partem' and 'due process'---Scope---Any proceeding arising out of equity could not be decided without providing opportunity of hearing---Court ought to follow the principle of 'audi alteram partem' and 'due process' which were basis of administration of justice, especially when any order, if passed, might affect the rights of the entity not party to the proceedings.”

55. The defect is therefore not one which can be brushed aside merely because the petitioner has arrayed the Magistrate or other local authorities as respondents. The decisive question is not who physically performed the act, but whose statutory direction, decision or authority is actually under challenge and whose legal interests would be affected by the relief sought. On the petitioner's own showing, NAB falls squarely within that category.

56. The Court cannot be expected to determine the legality of an action attributed to NAB without NAB being before it. Nor can a binding and effective order concerning the continuance, validity or consequences of that action appropriately be made behind its back. The omission assumes greater significance because the petitioner seeks not merely a declaration of an abstract legal right but substantive relief affecting the property and the proceedings connected therewith. Consequently, the non-joinder of NAB constitutes an additional and independent impediment to the exercise of constitutional jurisdiction in the present case.

57. In view of the above reasons, this petition, being misconceived on the ground of territorial jurisdiction and on the independent grounds of forumshopping, want of candour and non-joinder of a necessary party, is not Page 53 of 53 maintainable and is hereby DISMISSED, alongwith pending application(s), if any.
